thread.title: Facebook Investors Face Bear Market as Trust Erodes, Rival CEOs Call For More Oversight

author: thestreet.com
title: Facebook Investors Face Bear Market as Trust Erodes, Rival CEOs Call For More Oversight
text:
Facebook Inc. ( FB ) shares are set to open near an eight-month low Monday , and may extend a decline that hived more than $50 billion from the company's market value last week, as some of the world's most powerful CEOs call for stricter government oversight of the social media giant following a data scandal that may have affected 50 million users.
Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) CEO Tim Cook told the China Development Forum in Beijing this weekend that "some large profound change is needed" in order to restore public trust in the way that personal data is collected and used by the tech industry, a view echoed by IBM Corp CEO ( IBM ) Virginia Rometty, who called for a new era in which "ownership of the data does belong to the creator". The moves follow revelations that a controversial political consultancy, Cambridge Analytica, improperly obtained user data from Facebook that it may have used to help sway the 2016 elections in favor of President Donald Trump.
Apple is a holding in Jim Cramer's Action Alerts Plus .
"I'm personally not a big fan of regulation because sometimes regulation can have unexpected consequences to it," Cook told the audience in Beijing. "However I think this certain situation is so dire, and has become so large, that probably some well-crafted regulation is necessary."
Action Alerts Plus holding Facebook shares were marked 0.14% to the upside in pre-market trading Monday, indicating an opening bell price of $159.41 each, the lowest since July 2017, and a move that would take the stock 19% lower from its Feb. 1 intra-day record of $195.32.
Facebook's public image has also taken a massive hit, with the Menlo Park, Calif.-based group taking out full-page ads in several newspapers in order to apologize -- again -- for what he has called a "breach of trust" as the Twitter hashtag #DeleteFace gains ground.
In fact, a weekend Reuters/IPSOS poll of American users of the social network suggests fewer than half -- 41% -- trust the group to follow U.S. privacy laws, a figure that falls far short of those polled for Amazon Inc. ( AMZN ) , Google parent Alphabet Inc. ( GOOGL ) and Microsoft Inc. ( MSFT ) . All three names are held in Action Alerts Plus.
Zuck has to use the Congressional playbook--hire an outside firm to investigate, one that Congress trusts... Short of that, it won't get blessed....
— Jim Cramer (@jimcramer) March 26, 2018 "We know this is an issue of trust. We know this is a critical moment for our company, for the service we provide," COO Sherly Sandberg told CNBC last week. "We are going to do everything we can."
"Mark (Zuckerberg) has said, 'It's not a question of if regulation, it's a question of what type,'" explained Sandberg. "We're open to regulation. We work with lawmakers all over the world."
Lawmakers on both sides of the Atlantic are keen to take the billionaire Facebook founder and his most-trusted colleague at their word, with both Republican Greg Walden and Democrat Frank Pallone saying Thursday that they will ask Zuckerberg to appear before the House Energy and Commerce Committee that the two co-chair.
"The latest revelations regarding Facebook's use and security of user data raises many serious consumer protection concerns," the Committee said in a statement. "After committee staff received a briefing yesterday from Facebook officials, we felt that many questions were left unanswered."
In Britain, where Cambridge Analytica is based, MP Matt Hancock, the country's Minister for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, told BBC radio that "it shouldn't be for a company to decide what is the appropriate balance between privacy and innovation and use of data. Those rules should be set by society as a whole and so by Parliament."
